analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to assess and report the impacts of AI systems used in major life decisions.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2025 with 32 Democratic cosponsors, the bill sits in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no action beyond referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring large companies to study their automated decision-making systems before and after deploying them. It covers algorithms involved in decisions about jobs, housing, credit, health care, education, utilities, and other major life areas. Companies would have to document bias testing, data sources, privacy risks, and how consumers can contest decisions, file annual reports with the FTC, and face enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose lives are shaped by automated decisions — job applicants scored by screening software, renters and borrowers scored by pricing or approval algorithms, patients and students funneled by automated systems. The bill also gives state attorneys general and the FTC new tools to police these systems, and creates a public FTC repository where people can see which companies use which algorithms and how to appeal a decision.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers facing automated decisions on jobs, credit, housing

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered companies to perform ongoing impact assessments of algorithms used for 'critical decisions' — employment, housing, credit, health care, education, utilities, family planning, and legal services — including testing for differences in performance across race, sex, age, disability, and other characteristics [S2].

Requires companies to document how consumers get notice, opt out, contest, correct, or appeal an automated decision, and to publish a public, searchable FTC repository showing which entities deploy which algorithms and how to seek recourse [S2].

Requires companies to attempt to eliminate or mitigate any likely material negative impact, documenting steps up to removing the algorithm from the market, with the FTC and state attorneys general able to enforce violations under the Federal Trade Commission Act [S2].
Builds FTC capacity by creating a Bureau of Technology with at least 50 staff and adding 25 enforcement personnel, with funding authorized for both [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large companies that deploy or sell algorithmic decision systems — firms with over $50 million in annual receipts or data on more than a million consumers — bear the cost of assessments, documentation, annual reports, and potential FTC enforcement. Compliance expenses could be passed to consumers through prices, and the largest tech firms are best positioned to absorb them.

drawbacks.text: Impact assessments are largely confidential: companies must file only summary reports with the FTC, and the bill says nothing requires disclosing the full assessment to the Commission or the public, so the outside world would see a limited subset [S2].

The bill's power depends entirely on FTC rulemaking due within two years of enactment and on appropriations for the new Bureau of Technology and enforcement staff; a rulemaking delay or underfunding would leave the mandate largely on paper [S2].

Compliance is a real cost for large data-driven businesses, and while small businesses are exempted by the $50 million receipts and one-million-consumer thresholds, firms just above the cutoffs face the same assessment burden as the largest platforms [S2].

A good-faith objection: mandatory bias-testing and documentation requirements could slow the release of useful automated tools, and the bill explicitly declines to preempt stricter state laws, which critics argue creates a patchwork for companies operating nationwide [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and growing problem — opaque algorithms making life-changing decisions — and its design is moderate rather than sweeping: it does not ban any use of AI, exempts small businesses, and leans on disclosure and documented mitigation rather than prohibitions. The main weaknesses are that most of the underlying assessment stays confidential and that the whole structure depends on the FTC writing rules on schedule. On balance, the consumer protections are meaningful and the costs fall on large companies, though consumers may see some of that cost in prices.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2025 on September 19, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S4].
The bill attracted 32 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican support [S3].
No further action — no markup, no vote, no committee report — appears in the bill's action history after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo holds: large companies deploying algorithmic decision systems face no new federal assessment or reporting requirements, and the FTC gains no new algorithmic oversight tools.

for.name: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 32 cosponsors, all Democrats.

for.name: 32 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; none of them chairs the committee to which it was referred.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Brett Guthrie (R-KY)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 19, 2025 and has not scheduled a markup, reported the bill, or advanced it in any way.

against.name: Technology industry lobbying groups
against.role: Major business lobbies for platform and AI companies
against.what_they_did: Have generally opposed mandated algorithmic impact assessments and bias-auditing requirements as costly compliance burdens; no member of Congress has cosponsored the bill from the Republican side.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits with a Republican-controlled committee that has not acted on it.

industries.industry: Large tech platforms and AI system developers
industries.note: Companies above the bill's size thresholds would have to test their algorithms for bias, document data sources and privacy risks, file annual FTC reports, and build consumer appeal mechanisms — direct compliance costs and enforcement exposure. Their interest in avoiding these requirements runs against the consumers the bill tries to protect.

Firms handling identifying information on more than a million consumers or devices are covered entities, and they would have to document where their training data came from and whether consumers consented — a direct challenge to current data-sourcing practices.

industries.industry: Algorithm vendors selling to large clients
industries.note: Companies selling covered algorithms to big buyers must disclose their covered-entity status to vendors and can face liability for 'substantial assistance' in violations, but the bill also offers voluntary reporting benefits for smaller deployers and requires the FTC to provide compliance guidance and templates.

The $50 million receipts and one-million-consumer thresholds exempt most small firms from the assessment burden, while potentially benefiting from clearer, fairer automated tools sold by larger vendors.
The bill grants state AGs explicit authority to sue on behalf of residents for violations, adding a new enforcement lever over algorithmic harms in their states.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to House committees without a markup rarely advance, and this one has no Republican cosponsors in a Republican-controlled chamber and committee. Its realistic path is that it stays in committee unless its provisions are folded into a broader AI or privacy package; the earlier versions of this proposal also never received a floor vote in past Congresses.
